utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleague Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Edina Residovic and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me appears my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Zdravko Mucic. I would like to apologise on behalf of my co-counsel Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom; I hope he will be with us later in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me appears Mr. Thomas Moran, lawyer from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I appear here on behalf of Esad Landzo. My co-counsel is Ms. Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now have the witness back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly remind the witness that he is still on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic, continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, before our session ended, we have talked about the fact that you have never been to either the barracks or the prison in Celebici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dzajic, you do not have any personal knowledge of what was happening, if anything, in that barracks and what kinds of facilities were in there, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have confirmed in front of this Tribunal that you have not been an employee or the manager of the public utilities company, Standard, in 1992, and that the facts you gave you based on the memory of your predecessor, Mr. Zebic, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dzajic, you cannot affirm in front of this Tribunal that these data are 100 per cent true, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you have never checked these data, have you, if not from the memory and the notes from Mr. Zebic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not checked anything, because I did not inherit any records so I could not verify. At that time, as I said, I had my work assignment at the company at the factory Unis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in fact you cannot know at all neither where nor how the persons from the certificate died, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzajic, you have heard that Mr. Delalic had left Konjic towards the end of November, 1992 and at that time in Konjic started some kind of a witch hunt. There were claims that he went away with a Chetnik helicopter and that he was on the Serb side. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were rumours. The town was under a blockade, blocked, so there were lots of rumours. As I said, I had my work assignment, and I worked around the clock, so I was not able to go out very much. There was also lots of shellings. But such rumours could be heard amongst the inhabitants of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions for you, Mr. Dzajic. Thank you very much. I wish you a safe trip home. Thank you. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence for Mr. Mucic has no questions for Mr. Dzajic thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly ask a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours? Mr. Dzajic, my name is Salih Karabdic and I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. I would like to ask you a few questions. I would like you to bear in mind the instructions which my learned friend Ms. Residovic gave to you. Could you tell me, please, as a local from Konjic, were you aware of the fact that in November 1990 elections were held for the Assembly and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the inhabitants of Konjic voted in that election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time elections were also held for the Municipal Assembly of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: On the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Were those elections free? That is, could all the parties have their candidates? Could there be also independent candidates? Were there also independent candidates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Was there, after these elections, also established a Municipal Assembly of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was constitute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did it elect its President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Its Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Has this executive committee taken over the power after the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Could you, please, tell me whether, if you know, whether that Assembly and these bodies, were they operational towards the end of 1990, in 1991 and in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they held meetings up until -- I do not know when the last meeting was held, but I knew they could meet and they could be operational up until the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you know that since the aggression and after the immediate threat of war was proclaimed, do you know that War Presidency was established in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the War Presidency took over the function of the Municipal Assembly, according to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did that Municipal Assembly, that is the War Presidency, function in 1992 and during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Since the elections, and during all those three years I hereby have in mind, 1990, 1991 and 1992, the years we are speaking of here, so was during all that time in Konjic a legally -- a legally elected authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did that authority establish that it has its internal affairs, that means its police, a security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did it function, did it work from after the elections and all throughout this first year of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did function, but I do not know well the internal structure. But, yes, there was -- the police did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These are all my questions. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Esad Landzo has no questions of this witness but we would like to express our appreciation for his appearing here. Thank you very much, Mr. Dzajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No re-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzajic, I think that is all. Thank you very much. We are very grateful you were here. So you are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for the end of this thing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls General Arif Pasalic. Your Honours, while the witness is coming into the court he has indicated to me that he wishes to address your Honours on the question of the subpoena. He is reluctant to testify at the moment because of a death in his family, and he says that he would be prepared to testify after the 10th November. I have told General Pasalic that this is a matter he can raise with you, as he is under order of subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let him come in. Yes, you can swear the witness GENERAL ARIF PASALIC, (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I understand you wish to address some words to their Honours in relation to the subpoena that has been issued against you, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: And you seek their Honours leave to address them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What do you have to say to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I would like to say is that I am very surprised that a subpoena has been proclaimed, especially because up until now I co-operated with the representatives of The Hague Tribunal. My country did not contest that I could co-operate with The Hague Tribunal, and what is more I was even encouraged to do so. I have recently had a death in my family. My brother has died, and my brother lost his family members during this war. In a letter I have asked for the postponement of my testifying in front of this Tribunal. I have asked for a reasonable delay, which would correspond to our customs where we have a 40 day period of mourning. By the subpoena my name appeared in newspapers and in the media and I was exposed to certain pressure. It appeared as if I was forced to come to The Hague to testify. That is why I ask the court to abolish this subpoena. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, the subpoena was issued on the application of the Prosecution, having given reasons why it ought to be issued. One of the reasons was that perhaps you were not co-operating sufficiently to be able to attend at The Hague to testify. I am sure the Prosecutor would have told you what prompted the issue of the subpoena. Did you complain to him and tell him this version of your story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said this to the Prosecutor, Mr. Grant, and I think that Mr. Grant and all the others know that I did not show any signs, or neither I have said, that I would not come to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is having this information from you, quite distinct from what was told to it at the application for the subpoena, and we base authority to issue this subpoena on the facts available to us at the time. Now, I refer to your unwillingness to testify after having been here as to a religious custom which excludes you from participation in public matters, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained in a letter that in my -- that my people, there is a custom that for 40 days I should be with my family and not to participate in anything that is not within the framework of our family. I simply ask for a period of delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a little difficult for the Trial Chamber, which also takes into account the interests of other participants in the Prosecution itself, and other matters affecting arrangement of court sittings, other witnesses, and measures to facilitate the trial. You are already here and I do not think it would make much of a difference if your testimony goes ahead. This is quite a different thing from involuntary attendance to give evidence. You are not on pleasure trip, you are here doing a duty towards justice, which is not an infringement of any custom. You are being helpful. I think your custom will take into account the fact of your duty to us and your relevance in the prosecution we are undertaking. So please ignore this custom for the time being, because I am sure it will not take too long for you to complete your testimony and be discharged. You will go back to your family within the week. I do not think the Trial Chamber is supposed to grant that application for you not to testify now because of other commitments in the period you have suggested may be difficult for us to accommodate that. So you might co-operate with the Trial Chamber and testify. So Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That was an application by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to say that I know that it is not my place to comment on this, but since the witness has clearly stated that he never refused to come to testify, I would like to know whether the court will rule on his request for the annulment of the subpoena, regardless of when this witness will testify. I am asking for the benefit of the other witnesses too. I have been reading the Sarajevo press, and I think that the Trial Chamber must rule whether the subpoena was improperly issued on the basis of incorrect information, and that is why I should like the Trial Chamber to think over the request of the witness and to convey its ruling to the public. I am sorry for intervening, but I am reading the media regularly, and the facts that were conveyed to you and which served as a basis for your decision appear to have been totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that, your Honours? Might I suggest to counsel that rather than relying on the media she relies on the facts. Counsel has been supplied this morning with at least some of the material relied upon by the Prosecution. It is very clear what information was relied upon. I suggest she reads that, rather than come to this Chamber and start suggesting things on the basis of things she picks up in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 31st August, 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where was that? Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Janjici near Zenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My background is Muslim or Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an officer in the former Yugoslav People's Army and I am now an officer in the Army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many years have you served as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my elementary education I joined the second military school for non-commissioned officers and after 1962 I first started as a non-commissioned officer in the former JNA and became an officer in 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your current rank and position in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the rank of Brigadier General. I am now head of the department for control in the joint command of the Federation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you stationed in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of April 1992, I went to Mostar and reported to the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I was Lieutenant Colonel, a rank granted by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Mostar, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reported to the Mostar Territorial Defence, I was adviser for military issues for about 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the purpose and function of that post that you had with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The function was to make suggestions regarding the organisation and defence against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, initially who was your Commander in the Mostar Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have a Commander. There was the Chief-of- Staff of the Territorial Defence, Hasim Semsudija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the structure of the Mostar Territorial Defence undergo any changes while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We adjusted the structure of the Territorial Defence, depending on the conditions of the Defence against the aggressor, and shortly we formed units in local communities. They were squads and later platoons, and then we developed a system of defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did your position in the Territorial Defence then subsequently change? Did you take up another position in the Mostar Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th May, I took over as Battalion Commander for the Defence of Mostar and I held that post until 15th July, 1992, when I formed the first Mostar Brigade and was its Commander. Later in November, to be more precise as of 17th November, I formed the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic at the time was Chief-of-Staff of the Republican staff of the Territorial Defence. I met him during the war, and I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know when he assumed the position of chief of staff, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere in May, I cannot recall exactly, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, are you able to give the Chamber some idea of the distance by road from Mostar to Konjic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Mostar to Konjic, if you are thinking of the locality Konjic near Busovaca, I think the distance is about 200 kilometres. If you go via Sarajevo along the Bosna River valley and the Lasva River valley to Kaonik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are talking of Konjic or some other town? The pronunciation is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do apologise, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, because there is a locality called Kaonik near Busovaca. As for the distance, it is 40 to 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the early part of 1992 -- when I say the earlier part, I am talking April through to July -- can you give their Honours a general description of the conditions affecting the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the structure of it at that very early stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From April 1992; actually, after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a Republican staff of Territorial Defence based in Sarajevo. Outside Sarajevo there were district and municipal staffs of Territorial Defence, which were rather dispersed and disorganised, because people of Serbian ethnicity and quite a number of people of Croatian nationality had left these bodies, so it was mostly Bosniaks who remained and in personnel terms they were not very qualified. In Mostar there was a municipal TO because the district TO was disbanded, it fell apart. At the time, we did not have a complete system of organisation or control and command which was in the process of being established. We did not have a constant system of communications, because these were intercepted by the sieges of Sarajevo and other towns. There were numerous paramilitary formations and armed groups, because the process of aggression was fierce, so that we had no choice but to set up an organisation in the municipal staff, in the form of an army, the beginnings of an army, as best we could. With the republican TO staff we maintained contact most frequently by radio links, short-wave links and by messengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What had happened to the former army of Yugoslavia, the JNA, at this stage, in April or May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I abandoned the former Yugoslav People's Army at the beginning of March and at the beginning of March I joined the Territorial Defence. The former Yugoslav People's Army had already changed its characteristics, concepts and structure so that it no longer resembled the Yugoslav People's Army such as it was in the former Yugoslavia. In that system of control and demand there were already evident signs and aspirations towards the establishment of a greater Serbia with a high degree of nationalism and hatred for other ethnic groups. People who were not pro-Serbian were dismissed from positions of command and who did not fit into this policy of a greater Serbia. I was one of them. Assignments were given exclusively to people that enjoyed trust, and units were already being used to block certain roads and communications to collect weapons from TO warehouses. The shelling of Sarajevo had started, the shelling of Mostar, road blocks were put up. In a word, a chaotic situation in which you had two signs; on the one side the former Yugoslav People's Army, which had changed its insignia from the five-cornered star to the coat of arms of the present Republika Srpska, and using the armament, artillery and all the weapons that were shelling communications, towns, villages, the innocent and civilians. For me the Yugoslav People's Army no longer existed. It had acquired a completely different form of organisation, and had been transformed into an army which was carrying out aggression against its own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the forces that were -- that did exist, that were arranged against the former JNA; you mentioned, in your evidence, that they equipped themselves with arms from former -- from Territorial Defence barracks and so forth. Where else were arms acquired from during that period, by those forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no TO barracks. There were barracks of the former JNA and there were warehouses or depots in which the equipment and armaments of the TO were stored, but these warehouses had mostly been emptied by the JNA, which took all the equipment and armaments that it could. We set up units in local communities, in hamlets, villages. The units were equipped with the armaments we had, hunting rifles and Carbines. In some cases, TO staffs did acquire weapons, as was the case in Zenica where they conditioned the surrender of armaments to allow the troops of the former JNA to leave. In some cases TO units physically captured weapons from the remnants of the JNA and we purchased weapons with the money that we had and that we received from individuals, and we procured those weapons in various ways. I can tell you only about the way that I got hold of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we mentioned earlier the position of Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the Chief-of-Staff. What were his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was Chief-of-Staff of the Supreme Command. That is how his function was called at first and he was the superior, or he had a command function in relation to all TO structures in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, to who did Mr. Halilovic report at that time? Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole was President Izetbegovic, according to the constitution and the law, so that he probably reported to higher levels of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to indicate to us the -- probably you cannot do it in relation to all of them, but the people who were the immediate subordinates of Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The subordinates of Chief Sefer Halilovic were all the commanders of district staffs, all the commanders of municipal staffs, commanders of units, independent brigades, that were formed, and myself as Commander of Battalion and Brigade were subordinated to the staff of the Supreme Command. As the Corps Commander I was also subordinate to the Supreme Command. This applied to all the municipal district TO staffs, the commanders of independent units, the commanders of certain groups; in some cases they were called tactical groups. They were all subordinate to the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think you said that Mr. Halilovic was your immediate superior in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in the latter part of 1992, did you receive an order in relation to the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around the 16th or 17th November I was in the territory of Zenica municipality on assignment to form the joint command of the army, consisting of the Territorial Defence and the Croatian Defence Council. I was informed that I should return urgently to the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade, where I was given orders to form the 4th Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That 4th Corps was to unite all the military organisations along the Neretva River valley. This was on 17th November, 1992, that I received orders to form the 4th Corp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who issued that order to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of staff of the Supreme Command, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the geographical scope of the new 4th Corps that was established? Can you tell us the municipalities that it took in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was to organise and encompass TO units along the Neretva River valley from the pass at Bradina to cover the units of the Konjic municipalities, the municipalities of Prozor, the municipality of Jablanica and the municipality of Mostar, as well as the other municipalities, Nevesinje, Gacko Stolac, Capljina, if there were any TO units in those territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you go about establishing the 4th Corps? What did you do in relation to it, in compliance with your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formation of the 4th Corps is a process which, within the system of control and command, takes some time in wartime; this period is much shorter than in peacetime. In view of the situation that existed at the time, upon receiving the order, I undertook to tour the units in that territory to establish contact with the commanders of units, to meet with them, and to brief them, if they had not already been informed of that, that they were now part of a new formation called the 4th Corp. I was to organise those units, and if they were already organised I was to establish a command structure. I was appointed the Commander, and I had a chief of staff appointed to me; as for all the others, I had to find the appropriate people and to give them assignments which had to be verified by the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a man by the name of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Actually I met Zejnil Delalic during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of how you came to meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date but I think it was the second half of the summer, after fighting in the south against the aggressor forces and the liberation of a part of Mostar. I met with Mr. Zejnil Delalic in Konjic once, once not of Konjic, I cannot exactly remember the locality, it was in the mountains, and once in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met him, do you know what position he held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that at the time he held the position of co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you understand by the term "co-ordinator"? What is that function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we wished to define in general terms the term "co-ordinator" in a military sense, it is a man who is supposed to co-ordinate measures, procedures, involved in carrying out certain assignments. I do not know exact what Mr. Zejnil Delalic as a co-ordinator had assigned to him. This must have been determined by whoever it was that appointed him co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the former JNA I think you said you had similar positions. What role did the co-ordinators play in the military sense in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav People's Army did not have this permanent post of co-ordinator. These were only provisional positions. A certain person may be appointed to co-ordinate a particular activity, but there was no permanent position within a formation that was called a "co-ordinator". Such an appointment would be issued on a temporary basis, because the word itself implies the co-ordination among one, two or three parties, or people in a certain assignment, so that in the former JNA occasionally a co-ordinator would be appointed to carry out definite assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in terms of the role that Mr. Delalic played as co-ordinator, do you know any details of the functions he performed in this role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which details I could describe for you. I met Zejnil as a highly respected man who played a very noteworthy role in the resistance; a man who in Konjic municipality was one of the protagonists in putting up resistance against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he performed a military or a civilian role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the war it is difficult to separate the military from the civilian activities, particularly in the kind of aggression that we had in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that both civilian and military tasks were all in the service of defence. As far as I know, Zejnil Delalic co-ordinated both civilian and military structures that existed in Konjic at the time. My contact with Zejnil was co-ordination and co-operation between me as Brigade Commander and him as Zejnil Delalic, a co-ordinator, to the extent to which we could assist one another in the exchange of opinions, advice, or in the form of any kind of material assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 67, please? Your Honours, I have made copies of these exhibits, so that if your Honours do not have copies of them you can look at it. I have also made a copy for the Defence. I ask that the witness be shown the exhibit. I am not asking they be marked, it is only to assist your Honours while we are going through these things. General, would you look at the document that you are now shown, Exhibit 67, and read through it, if you would, for me, please, and then I will ask a question of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the heading it says: "War Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Konjic municipality, number 01-21/92. Date: May 2nd, 1992. On the basis of the decision of the War Presidency of Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you. If you could read it quietly to yourself. If you could read it to yourself, so that you can be familiar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, are the details of that exhibit, that special authorisation, consistent with what you understand to be the role of co-ordinator, as you have described it in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me my opinion about co-ordinators, and I conveyed it to you. But this is a document giving certain authorisations to the co-ordinator. The President of the War Presidency and Commander of the military staff are authorising, giving certain authorisations to the co-ordinator, by means of this document. These organisations are reduced to three points. First, he is authorised to lead in negotiations and concluding contracts between the main headquarters of the region of Herceg-Bosna and all representatives to conclude all kind of agreements on acquisition of weapons and joint actions of troops on the front. Those are the authorisations given to him by the body that issued this authorisation and it is valid for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it consistent with what you understand the role of this particular person at that time, as you understand the structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The structure of Territorial Defence at the time was as I described it to you; and this authorisation, I am not competent to answer the question whether this authorisation was in the spirit of the valid laws. It is up to the personnel giving the authorisation to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This might be misleading. I think this document bears the date "2nd May". We have the notification by which he was appointed the co-ordinator; it is much later date, so this is nothing to do with his duty as a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I will move on to that. Perhaps that exhibit might be handed back, and you could look at Exhibit 68, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, having looked at Exhibit 68, is the appointment that you see there consistent with what you understood to be the way matters were proceeding, particularly in a military sense, in the early part of 1992, May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you are implying exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I will be more specific. The appointment of Zejnil Delalic is by the President of the Presidency; is that something you would consider to be consistent with the circumstances of the revolution of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that particularly early period in time, namely May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decision, or rather a document in the form of a decision, of the President of the War Presidency of Konjic municipality, Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic. He took the decision and it is stated in the preamble of the basis of a session held in Konjic, which means that the municipality, as the civilian authority, had decided to appoint Zejnil Delalic as co-ordinator of the defence forces in Konjic municipality. The President of the municipality and the competent bodies can answer the question as to whether this was consistent or not. If it is called "War Presidency", then it must engage in the question of defence against aggression, and the President of the municipality regulated the matter in the way shown in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if you look at the top of the page, it says, does it not, that it was the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the President -- just before we leave that document, the President of the War Presidency that is mentioned there, Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic. Did you know that person at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what position did he hold when you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was President of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you understand to be his responsibilities as President of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, as Battalion and Brigade Commander, I did not even try to comprehend his competencies. I was concerned with military issues, and my co-operation with the President of the municipality of Konjic and other Presidents was only to the extent that it contributed to the struggle against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And to what extent was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are thinking specifically of the President of the municipality of Konjic, I met with him several times. These were meetings, as in the case with Mr. Zejnil Delalic, when we discussed the situation, how to resist the aggressor, what chances of defence there were. We were most concerned by supplies. We had the men, the manpower, but we did not have clothing or food or equipment; and we were exposed to aggression. We asked the President of the municipality to provide the conditions for us to be able to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there any distinction between a President of a municipality and a War President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name itself is indicative of the difference. The President of the municipality may also be the President of the War Presidency and, as its name indicates, it probably decides about crucial matters in times of war. Questions which are of interest to the municipality, these are probably regulated by the constitution and the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They may or may not have been at that time, is that correct, regulated by the laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not competent to say whether they were or not, in view of the fact that it was a state of war and there were probably possibilities to do things pursuant to the law and some things even against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the municipality of Konjic, did you have dealings yourself with Presidents of War Presidencies in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have contacts with the Presidents of the municipalities of Mostar, Capljina, Stolac, almost with all the Presidents in our area of responsibility where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was the nature of the business that you had, the business dealings that you had with these Presidents, similar to the nature of the dealings you had with the President of the War Presidency in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, virtually the same. These contacts were mostly limited to defence from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Terms of their authority, as far as you understand; what authority did they have over military matters, in the early part of 1992, as opposed to when, perhaps later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what was their authority, their competence, but I, as Commander of that unit, that is the Brigade and the Corps, had the responsibility towards my unit. It was the framework of their organisation, and I had to report and was responsible to the headquarters, the staff of the Supreme Command and I do not know about their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said earlier in your evidence that one of the priorities in that early part of the war was that acquisition of evidence, and you gave some evidence about that, in terms of it being seized from various places; and in addition to that it being acquired, as well. I would ask you to look, if you would, for me, please, at document MFI121. I also have a copy of this document here. General, this is a hand-written document. It may be a little difficult to read. I would ask you if you, would, please -- it should be a hand-written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we be informed as to what this document is? I do not recognise MFI121 as an initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps the General can be given the original, not the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I only have the English version in the records, so I will mark the Croatian version and give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have provided a copy, I hope, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May we see that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might one copy be given to their Honours, and at least one copy to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object to this witness being shown this document. It has not been admitted into evidence. The document is from the seized documents from Vienna which is not yet proven. Therefore, it is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a standard procedure for documents to be shown to a number of witnesses at any stage in the proceedings and for the documents to be identified. If the General is in a position to speak to the document and express some view about it, then it is entirely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, have you had an opportunity to read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not up to now, but I have read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to express any view, having regard to the circumstances that prevailed at that time, that is on 7th May, 1992, as to the nature of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Has this document been shown to be in the handwriting of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has not been established as yet. It was a document that was seized at his premises, though. The document, your Honours, speaks for itself, and it relates to the relevant period of time. It was located at the premises of the accused Zejnil Delalic. We have already heard evidence of the processes by which it was obtained, through the officers of the Austrian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure. I do not remember any evidence of this having been recovered anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was this document addressed to the General?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he see it ever before?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What are you going to ask him about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am going to ask him whether this document was consistent with the processes at the time for the acquisition of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is a matter for argument. You have shown him the document of 2nd May and asked for his opinion. He has not received this document. You have not shown it was in the handwriting of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure that he is introducing it for that purpose at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not attempting to establish that it was written by the accused. There are two issues here, your Honour; there is the issue of admissibility, and there is the issue of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are asking him whether this document is consistent with his duties under the order of 2nd May. That is a question of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am not. I am asking him whether this document is consistent with the processes that were in operation in terms of the acquisition of weapons, which he has already attested to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I would object that he is being asked to testify from a document which is not in evidence at all. It has been identified, but nobody has ever moved to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure you start speaking to a document until he has said anything about it. He has not said anything. He will show it to him, if he can say anything and you take it for its relevance, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You really ask him for the construction of the document, you really ask him that. Consistent with his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am merely asking whether this is a document consistent with what was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a construction of the document anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I am to establish relevance, your Honour. Otherwise I am in a catch-22. I am in a situation where I am not allowed to show its relevance and I am not allowed to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just asking the nature of the questions you are putting to him. This, whether this document is consistent. You are asking him really to construct this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking him to construct it. I am asking whether it is consistent with the sort of processes in operation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To do that, you will have to raise construction of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is not impermissible when it comes to the establishment of relevance. If I try to tender it now I am confronted with the issue of relevance, I assume, unless there is no objection. If there is no objection I will tender it. So if it is admitted into evidence I will move on. That is all I am seeking to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With all due respect to my learned friend, the issue of reliability has not been established in this document. We have been through about the seizure, the nature, the provenance of these documents has not been proven, the authenticity has not been proven. Those, in my submission, are the threshold questions to admissibility. That must be proven first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed. It is only whether in fact you got it from anywhere, if that is the case how reliable might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, have you had an opportunity to read that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you understand what the nature of the document is? What do you understand it relates to, from your reading of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean the contents, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is your understanding of what the document relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I could do is to read it aloud to the Tribunal. It simply relates to what is written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not want you to read it out, if you would not mind. I would rather you just tell me what you understand, what the contents of the document mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is getting kind of strange. He is being asked, now, to say what he thinks an unauthenticated document, with no proof as to where it came from, whether it is authentic or not, whether it was written by Zejnil Delalic or not, or who it was written by. He is now being asked to give this Tribunal his opinion about what it might mean. How can that be helpful, how can it be relevant? I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I did not understand it to be that. I believe he is trying to bring it to fall within the pattern. If he does then he might go for it; if it does not then I fear it might not be easy to establish then he cannot bring it in. It is the pattern of the procedure for those working within a particular formula. This is what he is trying to establish. He is trying to jump before he gets to -- until he attempts to link it with anybody. I do not know whether he can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am in total agreement with your Honour. Those would be the steps, but they are not the ones being taken. The General has just said the only way he can explain it to you is to read it to you because it only has meaning to him in the language it contains, that it has no other meaning to him. I think he has already said, "I cannot draw any conclusions about this, beyond what it says on its face", and on its face, as far as we understand now, it has no authenticity. So I cannot imagine that it has any value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: At the moment, the witness has answered nothing to do with it, therefore, so I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. There is one other problem, also. This witness is getting very close to testifying as an expert witness. He has never been designated as such. I understand by the very nature of his testimony he is going to call upon his expertise as a military officer, but when you start asking questions, "what is your opinion about this" ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are getting it a bit too awkward. When a General testifies about formations I do not know what else you can say, whether you designate him as an expert or not, a General is competent to disclose things about the formation of any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So he is competent to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We are not contesting his competency, we are contesting his designation as an expert under the order of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think that will matter. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, looking at that document, are you able, or are you not in a position to say whether it is consistent with your understanding of the way procedures were in operation in the very early part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object, your Honour. That is the previous question that was answered: "The only thing I can do is read it aloud to the Tribunal". It simply relates to what is in it. The same question has been answered by this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have asked him to explain, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that your answer? Let us hear your answer. If you are unable to fit it into any pattern, then there it ends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period from which this document is dated, I had no superiority from any kinds of units on the territory of the Konjic municipality. The only thing I can say about this document is what it appears to me, according to its form and its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it appears to you, according to its form and contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I renew my objection, your Honour. He is asking the witness to say what the document says. He is asking him to speculate on what it might mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not a question of speculation. The witness has already attested to the procedures in operation at the time in relation to the contents of what this document relates to. I mean, what the Defence are trying to do is they are trying to prevent any evidence whatsoever coming out on these documents so that your Honours are totally left in the dark about what they contain. Then when the Prosecution seeks to tender them they are going to jump up and immediately say, "they are not relevant, your Honours have heard no evidence as to relevance. " That is what they are trying to achieve. That is why they are objecting now to any discussion on it. In my submission that is an impermissible way to deal with it. The witnesses are entitled to give evidence which goes to the relevance of the document. That relevance is to be taken into consideration when we seek to tender it and admit it as an exhibit. We are not trying to seek to admit as an exhibit through this witness. This is not the witness through which this document will be tendered. It is entirely permissible for the witness to speak to the document. It is marked for identification. When it comes to be tendered, your Honours, it is not taking only into consideration what has happened at that moment but everything that has happened prior, in relation to that document. If this is ruled an improper procedure, then what the Defence can successfully do is simply sit there and object to any discussion about a document, and then at the end of the day say that your Honours must not accept it because it is not relevant. Truly, in that position your Honours would have not have heard any evidence as to its relevance. The only thing that you could then hear is evidence from me at the bar table trying to explain to you why it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me say first of all that I resent the implication that there is an obstructionist conspiracy going on over on this side of the room. There is not. What each of us over here is doing is what we are required ethically to do, and that is to try to make certain that the Rules of Evidence are followed in the presentation of evidence in a criminal case against persons accused of very serious matters. That is all we are doing, that is all we have ever done and that is all we will ever do. If that turns out to be obstructionist that is because of the Rules of Evidence, not because of any tactics we are taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be the Rules of Evidence of the United States, but it is not the Rules of Evidence that have been applied in numerous proceedings before this Chamber. In my submission, your Honour, it is appropriate that we refer to the Rules of Evidence of this Chamber when dealing and addressing this question. One of the primary bases upon which evidence is admitted is relevance. It is 11.30, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Tribunal will rise and then come back at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please. Kindly remind him that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General Pasalic, before the break we were looking at document number 121. I had not received an answer from you in relation to the question that I put before the objection was raised; and perhaps I might ask that question again. Are you able to say, yes or no, whether or not this document is consistent with your understanding of how matters were proceeding at that particular time, with respect to the acquisition of equipment and arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. This witness has stated he was not in Konjic municipality on the date indicated on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question is not limited to that municipality. It is a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours have not ruled on the objection before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I do not rule on what you are saying now. I am only saying if he asks him a question which shows a pattern, it need not be confined to that municipality. If he can answer let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, under the rulings of this Tribunal we are asking this witness to look at a document which is not admitted into this evidence, which is contrary to our Rules and the ruling of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not contrary to our rules. Let him please answer. Yes, can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, can you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer. I can say that there were similar, or correspondence done in this way, and work done in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that document might be handed back to the Registrar. I would ask you to look at the next document, if you will. Might a copy be given to their Honours and to the Defence as well? It is document 122. Can the original of that exhibit be taken out? I have a copy here for their Honours, and for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am a bit confused about numbers. Are 121 and 122 court exhibit numbers, or do those refer to something else, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They are court exhibit numbers, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps before I just take you to that document, General, can you tell me: were you aware of the way that documents were brought into Bosnia at that time, during the early part of 1992, in May/June of 1992? How were they actually brought? That is documents others than those that were seized from the opposition, or seized from JNA warehouses, and the like. How were they brought into the theatre of the conflict? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. You speak about the documents that were brought in or something else, because you asked me about how were these documents brought in, as far as I could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do apologise. That was a mistake on my part. I said before I would take you to the document. I wanted to ask you a question about the movement of weapons and equipment for the army of -- the emerging army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The equipment that was acquired from outside of the former Yugoslavia, how was that brought into the theatre of the conflict, as opposed to documents that were seized in Bosnia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but you are speaking about the -- how were the, was the equipment brought in, and the documents that were seized. I can only say how I , as a Commander of the Battalion Brigade, and Corps, how I acquired the armament, and all the armament that was acquired for the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is not what was within my competence. I can only tell you how I worked. I bought for the money that I had and the money was given as a donation, and I would buy rifles and other types of armaments, mostly lighter weapons; and it bought it for my men. I bought it from the civilians who dealt in the buying of arms and I also bought it from enemy soldiers who would engage in such activities. I simply paid for that armament, and all the rest of our armament was acquired as war went on. Some of the armament was made by ourselves in our makeshift workshops. I can only speak about how I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your experience, did you ever become aware of weapons being purchased outside of the former Yugoslavia, for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you receive some kind of weapons if it came from outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina you probably conclude to the fact that it has been purchased somewhere. Bosnia-Herzegovina would not have been able to defend itself without receiving weapons; and I do not know how it did. I can only say how I got some weapons from my superior commands. They would tell me on such and such a date you would receive weapons and they would say go, take, you would receive it from such and such a person, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If weapons and goods, it does not have to be only weapons, but if weapons and goods were to be brought into the theatre of operation, and when I speak of the theatre of operation, I am speaking in general terms in relation to Mostar, Konjic, right down to perhaps Bradina, in all those positions in that area, where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was operational, if arms were to be brought in by road, are you familiar, having regard to the conditions prevailing at the time, namely May or June of 1992, are you able to say how those -- that equipment, whether the arms or other equipment, would have been brought into that particular area, by what route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina was done by the former JNA, and we had to turn ourselves to the territory where there were no soldiers who were our aggressors. That was towards the west. So from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina the Croatian Defence Council, we -- that is how we received our weapons, and food. There were various routes, various roads, that entered into Mostar coming from either Ploce or Listica, or Prozor. There are 10 or 15 roads leading into Mostar. What arrives via what route, it is difficult to say, but that is the general direction where most of it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at that time, the forces of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina in particular were allies of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If by that you mean the forces of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council was a military component recognised under the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was on equal terms, just as the Territorial Defence, and then the BiH army. They were the two components. We worked together and we fought together against the forces of the aggressors, of the former JNA and the newly formed Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you look, please, at a document marked Exhibit 122 for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have to object, your Honour. This is a hand-written note. There is no date. There is no indication this document makes any reference to the relevant period of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, I think that in relation to that objection this document from a reading of it provides an indication of the appropriate date. I say that for the following reason: your Honours, we know that the acquisition of arms and equipment at the very early period of time was a matter of high priority for the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we also know at that stage that there was a militarial licence, if I might call it that, between the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. In my submission, even though the document itself, it is true, does not express a date, it itself indicates the relevance period of time having regard to what we know already on the evidence, on the record, of what was happening on the ground at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is very difficult to reconcile -- actually, to whom is it addressed? And for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It appears, your Honours, to be addressed to Mr. Zebic, a General by the name of Salman. It relates to the very questions I have just been speaking to with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are into the very problem of the authenticity and reliability, which was our objection before the break. Until that is established, the unreasonable doubt, as your Honours have ruled it must be. Our submission is that these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Zejnil will be coming in to tell us what it is all about, because there might be some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There may well indeed. I am not seeking to tender it at the stage. I am merely asking questions about this document, the cumulative effect of which I will ultimately argue goes to the question of its admissibility. This objection may well be appropriate if I was seeking to have the document accepted into evidence at this point in time. I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, would you please -- have you managed to read through the document you were just shown, that is Exhibit 122?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to express a view, yes or no, whether it appears to be consistent with your understanding of how goods for military purposes were brought through to the theatre of military operations in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a soldier, and officer of the Army of the Federation at that time, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what I understand are military documents. The only thing that I can say about this document is just as much as I could say with the previous document, hand-written, and I can only speak on the basis of the contents. Whether the contents reflect the situation on the ground is something that I have already said. The equipment and the weapons were purchased in the best way we could purchase it, and this is a way in which it was -- it was sometimes done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that document be returned, please? Would you now -- might the witness be shown document, exhibit 123? General Pasalic, that is a two page document that you have been shown there. Could you kindly read through it, please, page 1, and then over on to the second page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you notice that it is dated at the top of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we at least wait until we have had an opportunity to look at it before any substantive questions are asked about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, do you notice at the top of the document that it is dated? Do you see a date that appears there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And on the second page of the document there is a list of materials mentioned. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is being described there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know what is written in it. I -- yes, that is a matter I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is that military equipment that is being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from your knowledge of what was happening in the theatre at that particular point in time, was this the sort of equipment that was sought to be acquired by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who acquired that equipment, and for whom, but this is military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was fully equipped and therefore not in need of any of this material mentioned, or was this the sort of material that the army was seeking to acquire at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I ask you, I am not here, please, as a witness who is competent for the army. What I can say is -- as a witness of what happened in 1992 as a Commander of Brigade Battalion and a Corp. This equipment is military equipment and I also needed such type of equipment at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it was not as though there was a surplus of these various types of rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has explained that he was not a general witness for that type of answer, so if he gives you an answer which fits what was possible, I suppose that is all he can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand your Honour. I will not pursue that matter. General, just looking at this particular document, and being aware of the prevailing conditions in terms of how the emerging army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was operating at that time, and from your knowledge of that, is this document consistent with the procedures that were in place in some areas in relation to the acquiring of equipment, military equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a certain way, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that document be returned? Now, to your knowledge, General, are you aware whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic continued to perform the role of co-ordinator for all of the period of time that you knew he was there or did, so far as you know, his role change subsequently, during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Zejnil Delalic, when I met him, had the role of the co-ordinator. I cannot tell you the date from when to when, but I knew Zejnil Delalic as a person to whom I could contact when in matters concerning the fighting against the aggressor. Later on, he was linked with a formation subsequently formed, which was a tactical group. When he was in charge of the tactical group, I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what do you know of the establishment of the tactical group? What was the purpose of its establishment? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the tactical group as a general term, or the specific tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think at the moment I will ask you about this particular tactical group. What was it formed for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical group on the territory of the municipality of Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor and Vakuf was established in order to organise the resistance against the aggressor, that is the Serb and Montenegro aggressor, which was the remains of the former JNA and the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the military advantage, if any, of establishing a tactical group? In other words, why was a tactical group established? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer in a general way. Tactical groups are transitional formations, temporary formations whereby there you would form a group, a certain number of units, in order for those units to perform a particular task. Once the task has been accomplished the tactical group has no need to continue to exist. In military terms a tactical group is an organised group of units with a very specific task. Once the task is completed it stops existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the advantages of forming a tactical group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who forms a tactical group has a reason to do that, and he specifies the tasks of that tactical group. If it was formed in this case to engage in defensive operations for the purpose of protection from aggression, then that is its task, and duty to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now the tactical group that formed in the -- that was formed and centred on the municipality of Konjic, do you know what military objective there was in the establishment of this particular tactical group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I do not know what the specific goal was, but I think that it was for us to organise ourselves in the struggle against the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would it have assisted in the strengthening and co-ordinating of the military facility that was available to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A tactical group is a military formation of a temporary nature. Co-ordination is an activity that is engaged in. A tactical group as a provisional military formation cannot engage in defensive operations without the necessary resources. It must have the manpower, the equipment, armaments and material. You have to feed those people, you have to clothe them, you have to equip them to be able to fight the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a similar such concept of tactical group known of in the former structure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was serving in the former army, I did not participate in any war, but in our tactical tasks and exercises we reviewed and used such terms, the names of such military formations, in designing our tactical tasks and engaging in war games.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the category and type of authority, duties and responsibilities that a Commander of a tactical group would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, I had tactical groups that I formed, and to which I assigned specific tasks. I was familiar with the Konjic tactical group, in as much as I knew that it existed and I co-ordinated with it to the extent to which I co-ordinated with the people who held important positions, such as Zejnil Delalic and other leaders and commanders of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know who appointed Zejnil Delalic as the Commander of the Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably the chief of staff of the Supreme Command, because it was subordinated to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And might the witness be shown, please, Exhibit 71? Again, I have a copy of this exhibit here. It is also referred to as document 118. General, would you please read through that document, please? Not aloud, just to yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you see the stamp that appears at the foot of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I again ask that Mr. Niemann wait until the Defence have received their copies of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. General, do you see on the foot of Exhibit 71 a stamp that appears there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that familiar to you, that stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the stamp of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Defence, headquarters of Territorial Defence, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see beside that a signature that appears, under a name that is given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, though it is not very clear. The copy is not a good one.
