utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you cannot read it then let me know, but if you can read it are you able to say the designation of the person that signed it? In other words, are you able to give the title, the position of the person that signed it, from your copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says for the main staff of the armed forces, signed by Mr. Halilovic. That is what is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You notice that at the top it is dated, the 11th July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does this appear to be a document consistent with the type that was employed at the time in relation to the appointment of staff in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document by its form and content is similar to the documents that we used, and as for the validity of the document, I am not competent to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that exhibit be returned to the Registrar as well? Now, General, you mentioned earlier in your evidence that you received an instruction from the chief of the -- the chief of staff, Sefer Halilovic, in relation to the formation of the 4th Corp. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the formation of this Corps have any impact, so far as you are aware, on the operations that were being conducted by Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received a written document for the formation of the Corps, dated 17th November, 1992, from the chief of staff of the army, Sefer Halilovic. This document indicates who will be the Commander and who will be chief of staff, and it orders the formation; and I was told that within that Corps, which would be called the 4th Corps, that it would comprise the units of Territorial Defence, that is of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the municipality, then the municipality of Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica and units formed in the territory of the municipality of Mostar, from Gacko, Capljina and Stolac. I was given a list of the units that would become part of that Corp. Precisely what type of operations Zejnil Delalic performed with units in Konjic I cannot say exactly, but I think that the formation of the Corps did not upset the defensive operations, against the aggressor in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there a relationship in terms of military structure then created between you and Zejnil Delalic as a consequence of your order from Sefer Halilovic to establish the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I received the order to form the 4th Corps, as I have already said, this entails a process, and in the subsequent period and days that followed I toured the units. I visited also the units in the territory of the Konjic municipality. In that period from November 17th, for the next seven days, Zejnil Delalic had left the territory of Konjic municipality in, for us, an unknown direction at that time. I did not meet with Mr. Delalic after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to the establishment of the 4th Corps, was Zejnil Delalic your subordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the establishment of the 4th Corps did Zejnil Delalic become subordinate to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He answered that question, he said he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not think he left immediately, your Honour. I think there was a few days. After you established the 4th Corps, and perhaps only for a very short time, was Zejnil Delalic subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told in the order that my Corps would include units which were then, until then, part of the Tactical Group 1 in Konjic, which means that those units became a part of the 4th Corp. As I did not meet with Zejnil again in person, he was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as he was command of the tactical group he was directly subordinate to the command, the Supreme Command and the chief of staff of the Supreme Command, Sefer Halilovic, until any future appointment. The units in Konjic, Parasovic Jablanica and Pazor were subordinate to me, these units and their commanders and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that Zejnil Delalic, at no stage, was ever subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had superiority over Mr. Delalic. He was linked to higher levels of authority. He did not belong to my formation and control and command, chain of control and command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, prior to the establishment of the 4th Corps and in the early parts of 1992, April, May, June, July, during that period, did soldiers in the then emerging army of Bosnia-Herzegovina hold rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have ranks at the time. We only had functions, posts, from the soldier, to the leader, Commander, and some other positions. Only later in 1994 did we introduce ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may not know the answer to this: but did -- were there some people operating in the theatre of war centred around Konjic and Mostar who had de facto authority at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period May, June, until the formation of the Corps, in the territory of Konjic municipality there were people with certain authorisation, such as the Commander of the tactical groups, Commanders of Brigades, Commanders of Battalions. It did not counter members of the staff of the Supreme Command. I met with Mr. Divjak, who was at the time a member of the staff of the Supreme Command, Vehbija Karic and other officers who were carrying out their tasks. I do not know exactly what those tasks were. Meeting with them I discussed only those obligations and tasks that related to me as the Commander of the Battalion and the Brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, still speaking about this period of time, were there formal chains of commands that existed and were they followed, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system of control and command in the Territorial Defence and later in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed. There was the staff of the Supreme Command and subordinated units. I, as Commander of the Battalion and later of the Brigade, was directly subordinated to the chief of staff of the Supreme Command Sefer Halilovic. Then all the commanders and leaders of subordinated units were responsible to me, and then they had their own chain of control and command. That is how it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, in that period, did structures exist for taking disciplinary actions against members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army who had violated military rules or codes of conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the Battalion and Brigade Commander I was responsible for any disciplinary errors and offences; whatever happened in my unit, as the Commander it was my duty to deal with it. As for higher levels, we did not have any military Tribunals at the time, nor any superior bodies that were responsible for discipline. But this was ensured through the chain of control and command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If disciplinary action was to be taken against members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, at that time and even after the establishment of the 4th Corps, were there any Tribunals available to hear these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The state of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted certain legislation from the former Bosnia Herzegovina when it was a Republic of the former Yugoslavia. Within the Territorial Defence and the BiH army, in the beginning, we did not have a complete system, nor any judicial mechanisms, but we relied on district military Prosecutor's offices and military courts, which existed in the territory of a district. In concrete terms, Mostar had a military Prosecutor, and a court. And both the units of the BiH army and the HVO relied on them. But they dealt only with serious criminal offences, whereas disciplinary action was dealt with within the commands of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you, if you would, to look at a video, Exhibit 114. I assume that that has been taken to the booth? It has not been. Your Honours, I will attend to that after lunch and come back to that, rather than delay proceedings now. General, how were soldiers and officers, particularly senior officers, held accountable by the Supreme Command? Was that in the same way as you have just described, or was there a different structure to deal with senior officers, at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. Did senior officers -- were officers accountable in a different way than the others? We did not have ranks. We introduced ranks at the end of '93, beginning of '94. But members of the HVO and of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were accountable according to their functions, soldier according to his, a leader according to his and a Commander according to his. Only later did we issue rules of conduct for the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina which specified responsibilities according to functions, and all officers, once they were given ranks, were accountable according to those rules of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, during the period of 1992, and if it varied you may say so, but if it was the same, could you tell us who had control over the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question? Was it at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I will break up the question. In the beginning of 1992, in April, May, June, July, during that period, who exercised control over the military police? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Battalion Commander from 13th May to 15th July did not have any military police within any formation. It had a protective platoon which guarded the command and carried out those duties, with the formation of the Brigade in July 1992, I was authorised to form a police platoon, and I had such a platoon. With the formation of the Corps, I formed a Military Police Battalion, and I was in command of that Military Police Battalion as the Corps Commander, and in the Brigade, the military police platoon was accountable to me as the Brigade Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the position was with respect to military police in the tactical groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must repeat what I said. The tactical groups are provisional formations, which include certain brigades, battalions and other units. If that Brigade has its own military police within its formation then that military police was subordinated to the Brigade Commander, and the Unit Commanders within the tactical group are subordinated to their Commander. I do not know whether the tactical group had a special police unit which was directly accountable to the Commander of the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the period 1992, firstly in the period when the Brigade was established, did you ever have occasion to carry out disciplinary action against any soldiers under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Battalion and Brigade Commander, I did have certain disciplinary errors or offences, and I enforced certain sanctions. But as a typical example, it was only after the formation of the Corps, in view of the number of units, did this problem arise, and did we realise that we had to deal with it through higher judicial institutions and in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So far as you are aware, with respect to Commanders of the tactical groups, did they have a similar responsibility, albeit that they were only established for a short period of time, to deal with matters of discipline in a similar way that you had, as Brigade Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any Unit Commander, be it a Battalion, a Brigade or a tactical group, must have their duties clearly specified, and their competencies. I do not know whether the Commander of the tactical group had a clear indications as to his responsibilities with respect to disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other persons who would have had this responsibility, other than the Commander of the tactical group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every Commander is -- has responsibility towards his subordinated units. As the Brigade Commander, I was competent and had responsibility with respect to my subordinate units. For my officers, my Commanders, and my leaders of groups, and for my soldiers. I could not give you an example, now. I had disciplinary action; when a soldier does something that is not in accord with military conduct, then I would ask his Commander to punish him, to dismiss him from that post, to appoint him to another post, to call him to task, to caution him, to criticise him, and the like. In the interest of better understanding, I must say that at first, and I am referring specifically to 1992, we did not have time to engage in minor breaches by soldiers. Operations were quick, the offensives were fierce, so that it was possible for certain individuals to commit errors without them being sanctioned. There was a realistic possibility of this occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Niemann we will have to stop here for lunch and come back at 2.30. You will continue at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down. Please remind the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you might continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would like you now, if you would, please, to look at a video that will be played on the television screen in front of you. I asked that the technicians in the booth play two parts of Exhibit 114, the first part being from the beginning of the video tape through to minutes 2.41. It is a very short segment. Also from the part 11.49 seconds through to 16 minutes and 29 seconds. I think those parts have been -- I also ask when the person speaks on the video it be translated into the English language by the interpreters. I ask you watch closely the video when it is shown to you. At the conclusion of the playing of the video I will proceed to ask you some questions about that, please. Can we start playing Exhibit 114 at 0.0 through to 2.41? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Interpreting interview on video). "I find it hardest talking about myself. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to greet the citizens of Jablanica, all of those I know and those I do not know and my friends in particular who have been my hosts many times during the war. I would like to greet Mr. Mujo Kolundzija and my very good friend in Prozor, Emir, who is now a refugee, and their families. And all the people that I know. I am glad to be in Jablanica. I have to say that I am a little surprised that we have not met before, but better now than never. "What should I say about myself? My biography is short. I was born on 31st August, 1943. My father was Rasim, my mother, Dulba. In a village called Janjici, near Zenica, where I completed my elementary education. In 1959 I applied to the then training school for non-commissioned officers, now called the Military Secondary School. I graduated in 1962. I was then stationed in Nis. After Nis, in Vranje, and then to Skoplje. I was in Skoplje immediately after the earthquake there. In 1964 I enrolled at the Military Academy, which I graduated in 1968. I was stationed in Zagreb, Croatia, then Serbia then Bosnia-Herzegovina, many different places. "I graduated from the High Military Academy in 1979, which I attended from 1977. I was a JNA officer until the end of March this year. I have had various duties from the Commander of a radar, observation and guiding system to chief of staff of the aircraft base and deputy Commander. My last post was head of the general military subjects department in the airforce academy in Rajlovac. "I am married. I have two children, a 20 year old son, who is with me together -- who is with me in the 1st Mostar Brigade. I have a 16 year old daughter. I am healthy. I weigh 88 kilos and I am 188 centimetres tall. There is nothing else special to mention. After your detailed biography" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we could move on to the second part of that tape I indicated, at 11 minutes and 59 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Interpreting interview on video). "Recently in Konjic some members of the armed forces were arrested. Among them some very important people, like Jovan Divljak and Zejnil Delalic. Just a small correction. It is not Jovan Divljak but Divjak. Divjak, I am sorry. Who else did you mention? Zejnil Delalic. The citizens of Jablanica probably know what happened. I personally was in contact with Konjic even before this incident, several months before. I knew Divjak as an officer of the former army. He used to be Commander of the District Defence Headquarters in Mostar. He used to come here to Jablanica and Konjic. I knew him from Sarajevo as an excellent officer who was an expert in his job. "I met Zejnil Delalic during the war. I used to come and pass through Konjic. I would ask for assistance for what I needed and gave them what I had. We were in contact and exchanged views. I did not know him before the war. We had to do what we did in Konjic. It was not done by the Commander of the 4th Corps, it was these fighters who did it, the people who feel those problems the most. "For a long time something that is not good was happening in Konjic. There were people missing, killed, there was uncontrolled exchange of detainees, there were no records on the movement of equipment or weapons ... and when the people realised that, the morale among the soldiers had dropped significantly. People began asking, 'who is Zejnil?', 'who is Pasalic?', 'who is Divjak?'. They began to be suspicious about the people who were leading them. When this lack of trust affected the morale of the soldiers on the front-lines the Commanders noticed. Then we sat down and discussed what should be done. Zejnil left Konjic. His Pavo, what was his name, he also left Konjic. We did not want them to leave Konjic. They know the reasons why they left. "We established a commission, started an investigation and found out some horrible things. Dirty laundry. From incorrect use and sale of food for soldiers, uniforms, equipment and weapons. About 15 or so people were killed, and there were no explanations for their disappearance. There were no reasons. When you look at all this and take into account the exchange of prisoners, detainees, these are dishonest, dirty things which directly affect the success of the struggle against the Chetniks. "We started the investigation in Konjic, because we were interested in Zejnil Delalic and Divjak, or because we did not start the investigation because we wanted to denigrate Zejnil. However, I have to mention that Colonel Divjak is not one of those involved. He came much later and has nothing to do with the people who disappeared, the exchange of prisoners and murders. Yet there are some misdemeanours which harm the image of a member of the Supreme Command. We thus isolated Divjak from the Supreme Headquarters of the army staff and placed him under our control. We will hand him over to the army staff and leave it to the competent staff to decide. We will, of course, admit what we have discovered. The entire case has been concluded and forwarded to the investigating judge, who is going to continue with the proceedings and inform the public on the matter. The trial proceedings will start and appropriate sentences will be pronounced against the people who did things which are not deign of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims, the Croats and actually the entire population fighting against the Chetniks and the wronged Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, when did you give this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the date, but I think it was towards the end of 1992, somewhere in the second half of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you give the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Jablanica, that was the internal television of the town of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you gave the interview had the work of the committee that you mentioned there already commenced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The committee had already been operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The information that you provided in the interview that we have just observed, where did you gather that information from in order to provide it in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That information -- I was given that information from the subordinates who worked in Jablanica and Konjic, and from Commanders of various units who would report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what you said in the interview, about this investigation, were matters in a state of confusion in Konjic, prior to the investigation being carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say that the situation in the Neretva River valley, and the same went for Konjic and Jablanica, the situation was very difficult, because our system of defence and the functioning of the civilian authorities were not completely established. It was very good ground for rumours. For example, it was Konjic and Bradina in the village of Repovci, nine young men were killed from the 7th Battalion and everybody was asking why those people died, who killed them. We could not establish whether that was done by enemy units or by somebody else. There were various stories and reports that there was not enough food, not enough equipment, that the equipment was going to the other side and this was very bad for the morale of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you find out about the matters which prompted you to establish the commission of inquiry and investigation, committee of investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not remember the exact date when it happened. I received a report stating that the situation in Konjic was not good. I asked, "why is it not good?", and I asked the Commanders of the subordinate units and I was told that Mr. Zejnil Delalic had left Konjic, that he was not in Konjic any more. Since his role and the authority he had at the time we asked, "why was that?". So I went to Rasovici in the Neretva River valley, went to Ostroviz and Konjic, and I noted and concluded that within the town of Konjic there are military operations moving around, and their place was not there and the situation could -- was such that they had things among them they were trying to solve, and I said to Sefer Halilovic the situation was not good. He said, "this is your area of responsibility, try to establish what was going on". So I reported to him that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was not on the territory of Konjic and there are some other peoples we could not know where they were, and we were not able to establish what was going on. The head of the staff of the Supreme Command confirmed it, and he said that the Corps Commander, myself as a Corps Commander, I should establish what was going on as Sarajevo was under siege. We had to find out the truth. Then I decided to establish a committee that would investigate the matter. I knew how to do that because we used to do that in the former JNA in case we had an unclear situation. That is how I formed a group of people who were from my Corps and from the security centre in Mostar. I told them to go to Konjic and to investigate there what was going on, to contact the people and to report back to me. That is how that committee has started work. The head of the committee was my assistant for legal affairs, Muradif Hadzovic. He was a lawyer by profession. Other members of the committee were people from the Corps and also from the Brigade and Neretvica and also some people from the security, and that committee started work like that and the committee worked for a month and I received, from the committee, some reports from time to time. But these reports were still not complete, and not completely analysed. But the committee found that there were some matters, so we say, some matters that to our assessment at the time were not good. So we reported our staff of our Supreme Command about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you determine what you were going to do if you discovered that there had been any breaches of discipline or breaches of the law that had been committed? Had you determined what action you were going to take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was five years ago. Time has gone by, and it is difficult for me to remember the details of what I decided at the time. But I probably decided to do what I subsequently did. When the committee has finished with this investigative part, then we asked the staff of the Supreme Command to give us the right to arrest certain people and detain them for a while in order to be able to investigate the matter. One day, I think, we had 12 or 13 people which we had to arrest and keep detained for 30 days or more, and we did it at Parasovici, at the elementary school, so that these people could give their opinion about particulars. So we did it and there were reports that money matters were not settled. There were -- that there were food and supplies that were missing, some material and food was missing, and also we heard that there were cases of people who died and the causes were unknown. This was by the people who were in Celebici, the former warehouse of the JNA. That was in the village of Celebici. When we discovered that, I asked from the staff of the Supreme Command that we start criminal proceedings, because we thought there should be a criminal investigation about that. We also asked that a warrant, a search warrant is -- a warrant for the arrest for some people be issued, for people who left the territory, and so I started criminal proceedings in Zejnil Delalic and some other people so that the criminal proceedings that were started -- we did not prejudge somebody's guilt, but we wanted to know who did what, and wanted to make things clear. Later on, these criminal charges were given to -- over to the court, and the court was competent for the rest of this matter. People who were in the warehouse in some kind of detention or prison, or how it is called now, in the case of the Celebici, "camp" -- I do not know the details, but I know that people were found there. I was not in Celebici, I never even wanted to go there, but I ask the command as a soldier and officer it was not within my competence. I think I also signed an order that people should be handed over to the civilian authorities for further investigation and proceedings. This is all I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when the investigation had been conducted there, in the Konjic area, in particular what was the investigation focused on? Was it focused on the civilian side of things or on the military side of things, or on both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were focusing on the military aspect, and, in the meantime, certain parts of it covered also civilian aspects. You see, at that time the situation was such that there was no clear-cut division between military and civilian structures. We were trying to investigate the military aspect. Sometimes, maybe, we also covered some civilian structures, but that was only in order to establish facts of truth that would allow us to take adequate measures. I wanted, as a Corps Commander as well, that the unit -- that where a part of the 4th Corps, especially those units that were formerly already in the Corps, that everything would be cleared as to all the events that might have happened before, in case there were any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The former JNA base at Celebici, was that considered a military establishment or was it a civilian establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the Celebici warehouse, because I passed many times by. It was a JNA warehouse, where the specific task there were -- with a specific objective. There were some supplies there and materials there in the warehouse. But I do not think that later that was a military establishment. But we were trying to clear that matter later on, because some people linked it to the military, because I never saw there was a military prison there, and I had no data, I had no information -- who were these prisoners -- but we had to find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you conducted this investigation, do you know whether or not any evidence had been discovered of whether or not the persons in positions of authority in Konjic had carried out disciplinary action against subordinates for breaches of discipline? Did you discover any evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that the President of the commission who was in charge of the investigation reported to me that anybody had to do any disciplinary measures that were taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in particular did you discover whether or not any disciplinary action had been taken by the Commander of the Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that I was told of any disciplinary action having been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Going back, if I may, to the point in time prior to the establishment of the -- prior to the establishment of the 4th Corps, you spoke, in your evidence of the various responsibilities and so forth of a Tactical Group Commander. Would such responsibilities, in your experience, extend to such things as providing logistical support in relation to food and such other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the Commander of a Tactical Group, that his responsibilities depend on the assignments given to him by the person who appointed him. If the Commander of the supreme staff appointed him, then he probably indicated what his responsibilities would be. But in my view, he had to take care of the material needs of the members of his Tactical Group. He should have, at least. If this was not clearly specified, or if it was indicated that somebody else would take care of that, then that person had to co-ordinate activities with the Commander of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the period of time when you were located in Mostar, did you become aware of an operation with the title "Operation Jud", meaning "south"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that a structure was formed to carry out the Operation Jud. I think it related to the liberation of Sarajevo. That was in the summer of 1992. But I did not take part in that structure, nor in that operation. But I have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask you to look at the document that you are now shown. This one has not been introduced as yet, so there is no exhibit number. I would ask that it be given an exhibit number. Might a copy also be given to the Defence, and to their Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 187, Prosecution Exhibit 187.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, would you look at the document I have now had handed to you? Could you read through it please, to yourself, so that you can familiarise yourself with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Having regard to your understanding of the responsibilities and duties as a Commander of a Tactical Group as you understood it, are the orders contained in the documents you are now shown, Exhibit 187, consistent with what you would expect of a Commander of a Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I must repeat that I was not responsible nor competent for Tactical Group 1. If you are asking me as a military man to interpret this order or this document, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps tell us the contrary. Is it inconsistent with what you would expect to be the duties and responsibilities of a Commander, if that is the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it is consistent with the obligations of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have that marked for identification, if your Honours please. I understand, your Honour, that the video that was shown, Exhibit 114, has already been admitted and accepted into evidence. I might just check that, otherwise I will seek to tender it, at this stage. Perhaps the Registrar might assist me with that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has been admitted into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Again, General, during the period of time when you were stationed in Mostar, and indeed after the period of time that you became Commander of the 4th Corps, were you aware of an operation, military operation, being conducted in and around the area of Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that TO units after the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the territory of Konjic municipality, did fight against the remnants of the JNA the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors to defend the territory, or rather the town of Konjic. Those battles were also fought in the town of Borci. I am aware of that, but I do not know any details about these battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who is responsible, important in terms of command for the operation that was being conducted in Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the actual command of those operations, I do not know who was directly responsible. That was not within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know -- well, do you know, in fact, whether the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was operational at all in that area, in Borci? Perhaps you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, we were as the army of BiH and the HVO, we were -- had some kind of co-ordination in joint operations against the common enemy. I am not aware of any other formations except for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were some HVO units, but of what magnitude, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for co-ordinating the army units of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I am not able to say who was responsible for the co-ordination. Perhaps the person who ordered it might know. I know that the people in Konjic were fighting against the aggressor for the purpose of defence; but who exactly co-ordinated those activities, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I would ask you to look for me, please, at the next document, which is somewhat longer. It is Exhibit 124. I also have copies for their Honours, and a copy for the Defence. This is a lengthy document, General, but I would ask you, as quickly as possible, to read through it, if you would for me, please. Have you managed to look at that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Firstly, can you see the person that it appears to be addressed to, a Fahrudin Radoncic. Have you known that person? Did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Fahrudin Radoncic. He was for a time, at that time, I think, one of the secretaries of the Supreme Command staff of Sefer Halilovic. Today he is the owner, editor and one of the owners, of the daily newspaper, Avaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And he was located at the time, this was when this was written, December 1992, the date that is shown there, he was located in Sarajevo, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Sarajevo. I met him at Sefer Halilovic's. I do not know what function he held. I think he was one of Sefer Halilovic's secretaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the supreme -- those initials that appear there, the SVKOSR BH, that stands for the Supreme Command Staff Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, only it is not written correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How would it be if it -- perhaps you might tell us how it would be if it was written correctly. What would be there if it was written correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Staff of the Supreme Command, "OS", should be separated, and there should be an "I" between "B" and "H", "Bosnia-Herzegovina". I am thinking of the form and the grammar. I am looking at things militarily. First, it should be the "Stab" of the commander, that is the staff of the Supreme Command. "OS" means "armed forces"; then Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the chief of staff of the Supreme Command was Sefer Halilovic at that time, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was chief of staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, there is a reference there, in the second paragraph, to a meeting that took place on the evening of the 25th November, 1992, and there is a reference there to "A Pasalic", which I assume to be you, as attending that meeting. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that this document that we are now reviewing, in the heading it says "Tactical Group 1". At the time, there was no Tactical Group, it had already been incorporated into the 4th Corps, by 8th December. Secondly, in the document itself my surname and initial is mentioned, as well as a meeting. I think that I held that meeting in Prozor, when we discussed the problems linked to the aggression of the extremist section of the HVO against the Prozor. People were expelled and that is when we held that meeting -- if that is the reference to that meeting, and probably it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those people expelled were Muslim citizens, were they, at Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly Bosniaks, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not Zejnil Delalic was to attend that meeting, at any stage? Was it your expectation that he would have attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he did not attend at that meeting. That meeting he did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would it have been appropriate, having regard to the responsibilities and duties of Zejnil Delalic, to attend that meeting, had he chosen to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation at the time required, and that is also my opinion, that he should not attend, considering the revolt of people towards others. This need not necessarily always have been correct, or heartfelt, but it existed, because Prozor saw the extremist HVO members barge into their village, burn it down, expel them, and they were highly indignant that no one had assisted them. They were indignant that they had experienced this, and since they were within the Tactical Group, I felt that Zejnil Delalic should not attend, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a reference there, in the same paragraph, in the second sentence, where the author said: "I had agreed with others not to attend the meeting in order to forestall the allergy that the HVO was prone to develop when I was around." Were you aware of any tensions that existed between Zejnil Delalic and the HVO, either at this time or prior to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already after the aggression of the extremist section of the HVO against Prozor there was tension generally between the BiH army and the HVO in those areas. There was an aversion between me and the HVO and vice versa and also between Zejnil and the HVO, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if you go to the second page for me, please, General, and in about the centre of the page, immediately above the numbered paragraph 3, there is again a reference to Arif Pasalic. Do you see that reference there? It may be slightly different on your copy. I might just check that. It may not be the centre of the page. It is immediately above the number 3. It is towards the bottom of the second page on your copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see the reference there to yourself. That sentence: "Only a couple of days earlier Arif Pasalic suggested I should leave the area for a while and recommended a way to do it." Do you remember saying that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to Zejnil Delalic in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we are talking about now was occurring at a time when the situation in Konjic and Jablanica, and generally in the Neretva valley, between the HVO and the BiH army forces, and when the territory of Konjic, Jablanica and Prozor -- the situation was rather vague and unclear. At that time, as the Commander of the Corps, and before that as Brigade Commander, I was exposed to a series of dangers, and it was probably thanks to chance that I avoided being assassinated. I know that Zejnil Delalic had similar assassination threats. In the town itself there were several explosions which looked as if his life might be threatened and I advised him to withdraw for a while, that it was dangerous for him and his own life, and I felt it necessary to tell him that as a person, and as a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you suggest to him where he should go and how he should get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not suggest that. All that I said was what I have just told you, and I know that we discussed how we should move around in the territory controlled by the HVO and I told him at the time: use the method that I am using. You have to have documents under another name, and the most logical choice would be a Croatian surname and their documents to be able to move around freely. That is something that I did too, because there was no other way. I helped him to have a document like that. I think it was an ID card, I do not remember exactly. I gave him that document in an envelope. I did not know what was the name used on that ID, but it carried his photograph. We had those documents made to be able to move around in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in the area of the territory under the control of the HVO, because at the time and in that territory there were checkpoints at every so many kilometres, held by various units. There were quite a number of paramilitary formations, and if you did not have valid documents you could experience some very serious unpleasantness or even your life could -- life could be endangered. It was in that sense that I advised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, the paragraph numbered 3, which is immediately underneath the part that you have just been talking about, you just considered, there is a reference there to rumours in Croatian newspapers about Zejnil Delalic having flown in a helicopter. Did you ever hear any of that, any rumours of that, sort or any information of that sort, after he had departed on 25th November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was informed that Zejnil Delalic had left the territory of Konjic municipality, I personally did not know where he had gone, nor how. The people who informed me of this did not know either. I do not know what appeared in the Croatian newspapers at the time, but in some of our own newspapers and local radio stations there were various versions. At the time, it was very difficult to have any control over them, and nobody answered for any false reporting. And there were such versions; even on the radio I heard somebody reporting that I had reliable data to show that he had left by helicopter. This is something that I never stated. I do remember that there were such articles and reports that he had left by helicopter, in this way and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, General, just going to the signature part of the document that you have in front of you, at the end of the document, there appears the name "Fire", "F-I-R-E". Do you know what that is intended to represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what it means, used in this context; whether it is pseudonym or something, I do not know. I am not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to assist me again, I might ask the Registrar, I think that one has been admitted into evidence as well, that document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: According to my list, it was admitted into evidence by oral decision of the Trial Chamber on 12th September this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe the Registrar has made a mistake there, your Honours. This is one of the documents among many which has not been admitted into evidence. That is my understanding of your decision on September 12th of this year.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document was admitted into the list in the month of June 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, your ruling of September 12th did not admit any documents. You admitted twelve folders, not the contents of those folders. We object to the admission of this particular document since it has not been proven. The authenticity of this document has not been shown by the Prosecution. In our submission, it is inadmissible for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My understanding of the matter is that it has been admitted into evidence so it would seem that it is now really a question of the Prosecution establishing its relevance; and if the Prosecution is unable to establish that then the consequences of failing to do so will follow. My understanding is that it has been admitted, your Honours, as with all of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it was one of the documents in the folders, we were specific that none of the documents was concerned in the question of the admission of the folders themselves, because there was no nexus between the documents in the folders and what was admitted as the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So, your Honour, it was not that that was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This document falls into the category of document that was individually discussed and dealt with by the witness Moerbauer, not inside the folders. There was a group of folders that were seized. They were not tendered, at the end of the day, because the contents of the documents were not sought to be tendered, merely the folders were produced to show these were the folders from which the documents were extracted. It is not those documents. These documents are the documents specifically dealt with on an individual basis, one by one by the witness Moerbauer. My understanding is they have in fact been accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Moerbauer said that he examined this document from -- which you recovered from premises, allegedly occupied by Zejnil Delalic. He did not say this document belonged to, or bears the signatures of, Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I realise it has not reached that level of proof. My understanding is it is admitted into evidence from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Further documents found, that is all it is. Not that its contents are admitted as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am only going by the record. There may be some confusion about that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is possible to admit what he found in the premises, but in order to use it for evidence, at least it has to be authenticated first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand -- I initially had misunderstood the situation myself. I understand from our looking at the record that the position seems to be, as I understood it, that it has been admitted into evidence, but it has not -- but the relevance of it or what it seeks to prove has not yet been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is when you establish the authenticity of the document itself; then you can use it for the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, as proof of the contents of it. The technical step of admitting it ... I understand it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not possible to use it for its content until you establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be of assistance; on Friday, September 12th, at page 7407 of the transcript, in your decision from the bench, you said: "The Prosecution is seeking to tender twelve folders containing documents but not the documents contained therein." The document we are referring to, according to the testimony of Officer Moerbauer was found in folder I5, which he claims was handed to him by Officer Navrat. Also, during Officer Moerbauer's testimony, he was unable to identify any document from Inda-Bau which he claims he analysed at police headquarters. By the Prosecution's own witness, Officer Moerbauer, who claimed to have marked these documents, none of the documents alleged seized from Inda-Bau was identified in this courtroom by Officer Moerbauer. The Prosecution has failed to prove authenticity of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we appear to be speaking at cross-purposes. This is not what he is saying. The contention of Mr. Niemann is that these documents are different from those in the folders, and as I said even if Mr. Moerbauer had at that time removed this one and stated that these were documents recovered, it might be admitted as documents they have recovered, but he can not use them for the contents of the documents. This is what we are saying. That is quite different from what you are arguing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the evidence, your Honour, the Prosecution witness Moerbauer says this document was in folder I5. That can be found on page 3653 of the record. I do not know how my friend can be contending this document comes from any other place other than I5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the confusion was there were twelve folders that were presented to the court. Those documents were not admitted, and those folders were not admitted into evidence, and the Prosecution does not seek to tender them in as evidence. The only purpose they were produced for -- this was the chain of evidence issue. The documents that the present document, 124, relates to is the documents that were taken out of those folders before it ever came near this court and were dealt with individually by Moerbauer and others. It is my understanding that it is those documents that have been accepted into evidence. Now, I understand the issue, that they cannot be relied upon as proof of their contents until they are proved. But I understand they have been admitted, so the formal process of admitting the document has taken place. That is the only thing that concerned me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think this is where my learned friend and I part company, because this document from the testimony of Moerbauer allegedly comes from folder I5. It does not come from anywhere else. Moerbauer says he was handed that folder among the twelve he allegedly received from Navrat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All that you are saying is that no such evidence occurred, that Moerbauer had moved documents outside those twelve folders. No such evidence was before the Trial Chamber that there were documents outside those folders which he says he recovered. Is it your argument that all the documents which you can rely upon here, are documents which were in the folders? That is not what is being said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This particular document was in folder I5, according to the testimony of Moerbauer. When he came before this court he could not identify a mark which he said he placed upon every document within I5. This document has not been authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Everybody has agreed that it cannot be used for the contents. So I cannot see your argument here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask the witness be shown this document. I have a copy, and an English version. It is a document that has not as yet been tendered. I ask that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the document of the Prosecution 188, 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I ask that this document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you sure this document relates to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I noticed that, your Honour, yes. Paragraph 3, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am looking at the last page, it is signed by Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, there is some degree of overlapping. General, I would ask you to look through that particular document you are being shown there. In particular, I am asking you to concentrate on the paragraph numbered 3, which appears on the second page of my version of the document, and appears towards the bottom of the second page of your document. General, starting off with going to the signatory side of that part of that document, at the very bottom, on the last page, did you know that particular Commander at the time when you were located in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And insofar as the responsibilities of Zejnil Delalic were concerned, was there an overlap, or I should say a mutual area of responsibility, consistent with the area of responsibility of Colonel Blaskic, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Blaskic was the Commander of the operational zone of central Bosnia, the headquarters of which were in Vitez, and under his responsibilities were the Croatian Defence Council unit, but there were also BiH army units there towards Gornji Vakuf and Prozor. I am not sure whether Prozor was in his area, but there were units which overlapped in the zones of responsibilities, the areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You see in relation to paragraph 3 in particular, a reference there on 7th, 8th August, which I assume is 1992, there is a reference to hostility by TO members in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is said in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall any incidents occurring in this area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was one of the eyewitnesses of the conflict between the BiH army and the HVO, which happened first on 24th October, 1992, when the extreme section of the HVO attacked Prozor. I was in Prozor at that time. I was also in Novi Travnik when the conflict started between the BiH army and the HVO. I heard of the conflict in Kiseljak but I was not there. Here it speaks of aggression. On 9th May I was informed I performed aggression on the HVO and asked of Bosniaks to have white flags and to surrender. It is wrongly used word here or maybe done on purpose like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not asking whether or not you agree with the terminology employed, indeed I would be surprised if you did. I am just asking whether you were aware of any conflict that was arising in those places. I want to specifically move on to the reference there to the conflict brewing in Jablanica; were you aware of a conflict developing in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, to the relevance of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes specifically to -- it needs to be read, I think, to see the reference of it. It makes specific reference to Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware of conflict brewing in that particular area at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And there is also a reference there to a demand by Zejnil Delalic when he speaks and says here, I will quote it: "... speaks of HVO members of gangs of hooligans and talks of a need to disband the HVO." Were you aware of allegations of this time being made at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: By Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read this for the first time here. I never heard of such allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear allegations coming in the other direction, from the Muslim side or the army of the BiH side, saying that incidents were happening with members of the HVO, at that particular period in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period of time, that happened somewhere around 11th August, 1992, there were stories about the conflicts between the army and the Croatian Defence Council. The comments were different. Everybody had their own opinion. Those people who wanted common fighting against the Chetniks were against such conflicts. We were trying to prevent those conflicts, under orders of our superior commands, but these conflicts continued to happen, and they are the result of various objectives of fighting, and struggle. And they did happen, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, would you -- perhaps that document might be handed back. It is to be marked for identification. I am not seeking to tender it at this stage. Would you look, please, at the document that you are now shown? Might a copy be given to their Honours, and a copy to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we be reminded of the number of the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 188, your Honour. Might this document be given a number too, please, the one you are now being shown?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think this should be 189.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This was a previous document. Yes. This is 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, in your evidence just immediately prior to showing you this document, you have spoken of the increasing tensions between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a number of areas, including the area of Prozor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also spoke of a meeting that you attended of the refugees of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see this order that has now been shown to you, and from a reading of that order does that appear to be consistent with the worsening or deterioration of the situation in the Prozor area, and does it appear to relate to that deterioration of relations between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO at that particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to mention that the witness spoke about a meeting towards the end of November, and this document is about August 1992, so it does not relate to the question that has just been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it might, your Honour. I do think that the refugees do not appear until after this military action. I address the question to the General. In relation to the second paragraph of this document here, General, it relates to the to evacuation the Muslim population. Do you see that reference there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The refugees you saw in that meeting in November of 1992, were they refugees that arose as a consequence of this evacuation that took place because of the deterioration of the situation between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The refugees I spoke of at the meeting in August were in Prozor, and those were refugees that had to flee under the pressure of the HVO which was already present in Prozor, with all its forces. The aggression on Prozor happened on the 24th October. At that time an even greater number of refugees were expelled, but already in the beginning, in July and August, people were leaving the area of the town under pressure from HVO and their units. These units -- those were the refugees I spoke of. Here it is exactly meant, the refugees, just as it is written, from a particular village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The position is not slightly clear to me. I have the order of appointment for Zejnil Delalic as commanding officer of the BiH army Tactical Group for the areas of Hazici, Kazaric, Konjic and Jablanica. This town Prozor, was it subsequently extended, the authority, to Prozor also?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am afraid I cannot answer your Honour, I do not know. I will need to find that out. I do not know if the General can assist us on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have seen that order. Prozor is not mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I draw your attention to the fact that the Prosecutor has in no way shown the authenticity or anything else linked to this document which could approve or show to anybody anything, at the least to this witness, because we do not know anything about the document, who did it, when. This is a very poor copy of the document. I think that the Prosecutor has no grounds for using such a document even throughout his examination, let alone to tender it to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, firstly I am not seeking to tender it through this witness. Secondly, it is appropriate that the witness be shown a document that relates to the deterioration in relations between the HVO and the BiH armed forces. It is appropriate for the Prosecution to present this, having regard to the fact that the witness has attested to the events that occurred subsequently in Prozor. It is appropriate, your Honour, that the witness be shown this document, notwithstanding its quality, having regard to the fact that this is the best copy or quality copy that we were given. We have not deliberately set about the process of making it worse. So, your Honours, if this witness is in a position to express any views in relation to it, and I submit that he is, having regard to the evidence that you have already heard, then he should be permitted to express those views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, General, do you see the reference in the first paragraph to the withdrawal of BiH armed forces? Do you know why that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether this order had been realised or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any evacuation of Muslim populations having taken place in those areas that are mentioned there, at about the end of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that document might be returned to the Registrar. General, I would ask you to look at this document, which I will now show you. This is also a new document. Might it be given a new number, please, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, I seek to have this marked for identification. Your Honours, I note that it is 4.00 pm. Would your Honours wish to adjourn now and we will resume this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We shall now rise and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please. Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. General Pasalic, just before the break I asked you to look for me at document marked number 190. Did you manage to do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, in this document, the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object. This document has been marked for identification purposes. I submit the first question for the witness is to ask him whether he can identify it, not to ask questions on it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. General, in the second paragraph of the document that you have seen there, there is a reference there to percentages. From your experience in the field at that particular time, and in particular during the year of 1992, were you aware of any practices in relation to such matters that you are able to attest to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did that operate? What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the percentages taken by the Croatian Defence Council, I do not know what the purpose was. It depended on the resources being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did this come about? How were percentages of the goods extracted as goods were carried? How did that occur? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply through the territory under the control of the HVO. It was not possible to transport anything without paying for it. If you did not have the funds, then you had to give a certain percentages of those supplies to the HVO, to ensure passage through that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the consequence of not providing the percentages? What happened if percentages were not provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The consequences would be that you could not pass through that part of territory. Sometimes, the consequences would be that they would simply seize them under threat of a conflict, under threat of use of arms, so that you could no longer appear along that route, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, in the early part of the war, around May and June, that early part, were there any arrangements between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO for sharing or exchanging of equipment that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We generally had many agreements, but few of them were respected. I personally, as Commander of the Battalion, Brigade, and later the Corps, I had a number of arrangements with the HVO, but you would agree to something at a meeting and then in practice something else would happen. This was probably due to the arbitrariness of some of the Commanders of the HVO, but it was also due to the system of simply capturing parts. For example, I got a 122 millimetre Howitzer from the factory in Novi Travnik and the HVO seized it when it was passing through territory under their control. I never managed to get it back. There were also physical attacks. Outside the control of the system of the HVO and the BiH army a unit would intercede a driver transporting the supply and simply seize it from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the early time, in the early part of the war in early May, April and May 1992, when the relations between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not so tense, were there times when both armies agreed to exchange equipment and share equipment, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had examples of using, together with the HVO, certain equipment in the struggle against the remnants of the former JNA and the Chetniks, as we called them then. But we shared artillery, for instance, or we jointly engaged in combat against the same aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it necessary to, for you, in order to share this equipment, to be authorised to do that, or is it something that you could just do without authorisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the Commander, I could not go beyond my zone unless I had an appropriate document. I could not receive equipment if I did not have the necessary authorisation, and if I were to send my men to get equipment from the storage, from the warehouse, I had to give them a document, authorising them to take that equipment and bring it to the command of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the document that you are now shown, please? This is a document that will need to be given a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked Prosecution Exhibit 191.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We need to wait for a moment, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to Exhibit 191 and other documents that have preceded it, just for the purposes of the record, on behalf of Mr. Landzo, I want to record our objection to this and all documents that have been handled in this same way. My understanding of what is happening is that documents that have no showing of authenticity whatsoever are being shown to the witness and, even more seriously, shown to the court, the trier of fact in this case, with the representation that, by Mr. Niemann, that he is not even trying to tender them at this point. I worry how, when we get down to this Tribunal needing to make decisions in this case, you will ever be able to separate in your minds what is evidence in the case and what is not, because all day you have been reading documents that I think will never come into evidence, that the Prosecution has said they are not even intending to tender at this point; and I am worried about how that all finally works out. If it is the court's position that this is an appropriate way to present evidence, then I only hope that Mr. Niemann will not object when we begin to do and use the same procedure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am surprised that Mr. Ackerman has seen fit to suggest that your Honours may have difficulty performing the task of sorting evidence. I am disappointed that he has made such an observation. It is regrettable that he would do so. I am sure your Honours will have no difficulty in doing that when it comes to findings. At the end of the day I am quite sure that your Honours will be diligent in separating that which is considered and accepted as evidence from that which is rejected, or not accepted as evidence. I am sure your Honours, and I have great confidence, in fact, that your Honours have the capacity to do this. Indeed, in the jurisdiction where Mr. Ackerman comes from he is well aware that juries are often instructed to do it. If juries can be instructed to do it then I have no doubt whatsoever that people with legal training such as your Honours could do it without any difficulty at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I actually I am not surprised because many of the questions coming from all the sides ignore the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So that is the real problem. But I think we should be able to take care out of that. It will not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. General, do you recognise the stamp that appears on the base of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name of the person who has signed it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In printed letters it says "Jerko Doko, graduate economist". I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time he was Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke earlier in your evidence of a need to have authorisation to deal with equipment belonging to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is this consistent with the types of authorisations that would be required for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an authorisation issued by the Minister Jerko Doko in line with his function at the time and the authorisation itself describes what is being authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, do you know who it was that had ultimate responsibility for prisoners of war that were detained by members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concept of detention of prisoners of war, as the Battalion Commander and Brigade Commander I had prisoners of war which I captured in the course of battle, and I was responsible for them as the Commander, while they were in my unit, and I would hand them over to the headquarters of the HVO with whom we engaged jointly in operations against the same aggressor. The continued proceedings were within the terms of reference of that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And above you, who was responsible for prisoners of war in the -- who was your immediate superior responsible for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My superior at the time was the chief of staff of the Supreme of Command, Sefer Halilovic, who was responsible for the overall activities of the Territorial Defence and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were subordinated to him, within the chain of control and command. He was probably also responsible for all other matters, including the question of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have any responsibility in terms of the conditions of detention of prisoners of war that you had captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not have those responsibilities. At the time my unit was of such a level and rank that I did not have any competence over captured men. My duty was to hand them over to the responsible headquarters, and that was the HVO headquarters in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in circumstances where the HVO were not responsible, who would then be responsible for the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
