utterances.text: If they were captured by my unit, I was responsible as the Commander until I handed them over to the next level of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What responsibility did you have to these prisoners of war during the time that they were in your custody, that is prior to them being handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My responsibilities were those included in the general instructions of the Superior Command. Our orders were that prisoners of war should be disarmed, secured, escorted and handed over to competent authorities for further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During your training as a military officer, did you receive any special training with respect to the receiving and treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through my training in the former Yugoslav People's Army, through secondary military schools, the Academy and the High Academy, we had certain subjects taught regarding the treatment of prisoners of war. We reviewed and studied and were taught the Geneva and other Conventions relevant to prisoners of war. With the beginning of the war, we in the BiH army did not have any specific training, because there was no time for it, but we were given certain instructions regarding the treatment of the people who are captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were those certain instruction that is you were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To treat captured soldiers and people in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions, that they should not be exposed to any other pressure or arbitrary treatment by individuals, or any other group of people; that they had to be under the control of the responsible command, and should be accommodated in places specially assigned for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And to whom were these instructions given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were given to those of us who were in charge of units. I received such instructions as the Commander of the Battalion and the Brigade in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what would be the consequences to you, if you had failed to comply with those instructions? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the consequences would have been, but it is my duty to carry out the orders of my superiors. If that order includes instructions regarding the treatment of captured people, if I fail to follow those orders, actions are determined by my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you have faced disciplinary action by your superiors if you had failed to comply with these orders in relation to captured persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they could have taken such measures, but I have said what the conditions were. My superior, that is chief of staff Sefer Halilovic, at the time was in Sarajevo under siege. Our contacts were by means of radio and possibly by messenger. He probably could not fully implement all those measures, but he would have probably in some other ways sought to sanction my errors. I did not have any such example when I should have come under any sanctions, so I cannot say what he would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to discipline soldiers under your command for failing to comply with your orders with respect to the treatment of captured persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any such instances of soldiers treating prisoners in a way that would require any disciplinary measures in the period of the formation of the 4th Corp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, do you know why Serb prisoners were being held in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who the prisoners were by name, nor their ethnic or social origin. I was told that people had been isolated in the premises of the former JNA warehouse in Celebici, that they were there in the hangar. They told me I was told that they were mostly of Serb ethnicity, but I do not know individually. I gave the commission the task to investigate who those people were, whether they were members of the former JNA, whether they were soldiers, in fact to investigate who those people were, and to report to the competent courts for further proceedings. Later on, I required that those people from my area of responsibility should be handed over to the civilian judiciary authorities for further proceedings, and I think it was at the end of December that I actually did this with a written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, I would ask you now to look at Exhibit 137, and I have a copy for your Honours and for the Defence of this exhibit. General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear too well in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have also got noise in the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Try to make an adjustment and see whether you can improve on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will speak for a moment and see if you can hear me. Can you hear me now? Does that sound better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we will try to get one of the technicians to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any improvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, how is it that you recognise this document? How is it that you are able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my report to the staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, addressed personally to the chief of staff, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it is dated 7th December, 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you affix your signature to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did. It is not here, because this had been sent by fax, but I think that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, General, there are a number of names mentioned thereof, persons that you have ordered to be detained for 30 days. Firstly, the name Edib Saric; did you know that person yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met him in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to confirm whether he did indeed hold the position of Commander of the Tactical Group -- of assistant to the Commander of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he held that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next named person there, Hazim Delic, were you able, as a result of your inquiries, to establish that he held the position of Deputy Commander of the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The officers, the functions that were held and that are listed here are the ones I was informed of by the Committee for Investigation; and they have established that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a result of the commission that you -- the commission that you ordered, were you informed of the positions held by the next two named persons, numbers 4 and 5, Esad Landzo and Osman Dedic, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They informed me that these persons whose names first and last are stated here and that office, the duty they did, were on the territory of Konjic. For Esad Landzo and Osman Dedic there is no position that they held that is noted here, because I did not know what concrete specific duties they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And finally, down in the last paragraph, there is a reference there to the issue of arrest warrant by MUP, and there is also a reference to Interpol. Had you sought an Interpol warrant at that stage because Mr. Zejnil Delalic and Mucic had left the territory by that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At point 4, IV, I asked the chief of staff to give an approval for Zejnil Delalic as the Commander of the Tactical Group and Mucic as the Commander of the prison, so that the warrant for arrest be issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the MUP, and the Interpol, because they had the territory. As I was not competent to issue such a warrant I asked that from the chief of staff of the Supreme Command, superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that the only reason why you wrote to the chief of staff, to the Supreme Command, or did you report to him for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 4 is the last one in this report and the rest of the report is given under numbers 1, 2 and 3 -- I, II and III. The last paragraphs ask for an arrest warrant to be issued and also to start criminal proceedings and take criminal charges in absentia because the committee has established that there were elements for criminal charges against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you report this to Sefer Halilovic, because he was your Commander, your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The report is addressed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I might just ask the Registrar to confirm that this has been admitted into evidence, your Honours, please? Whether or not it has been admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document was admitted into evidence by the oral decision of the Trial Chamber on the 10th September, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, but what we have just heard does not -- is not consistent with the ruling in the transcript of this Tribunal on that day. We only heard by the Trial Chamber the decision about the legality of the proceedings. But there was, in no case, anything about the admission of any of the documents that were in the folders. To my specific question the Trial Chamber has answered, and this is in the transcript, that relating to every document it will be necessary to determine the authenticity of that document and relevance of the document and only then decide upon the admitting of these documents into evidence. If there was any difference about the decision of the Trial Chamber, we want everything to check why this decision of the Tribunal was written in such a way in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can we hear your reply, because you have before you the person who actually has claimed to have signed this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and I tender it, if there is any doubt about the question. Because he is here, we do not envisage him coming back. As he is the author of the document, he has described its contents, he has recognised it. I would tender it if it has not been tendered. Alternatively, if it has been tendered then, your Honours, I would argue that it may now be accepted for the truth of its contents, having regard to the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure it could be tendered by anybody else other than the author, the person who actually signed it, because I do not see how the authenticity could be accepted except by the person who actually signed it. I am not certain that it was tendered to prove that this was the contents of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it has not been, your Honour, I tender it and I ask that it be accepted into evidence of the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any objections let us know, because the General who actually signed it is before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this moment we have no objection to the admission into evidence of this document, since the General has recognised it. But I have an objection to every single document that has been shown up to now from those folders nobody has ever seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When a document has been recovered from someone it could be admitted as what he recovered. It does not contend the contents which have to be established by the person who actually made it. Now, here is the person who actually signed the document before you. I do not see what your arguments would be. It could be admitted in evidence as a document signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask also that Exhibit 114, the video tape, be admitted on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, because that is the person that gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He gave the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to 114, we have no objection to those portions involving the General. Any extraneous things that happened beyond there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Shall not be part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is our objection. We agree with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Just his interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct. We have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. General, I would ask you now to be shown Exhibit 141. Again, I have a copy for your Honours and for the Defence. General, have you had an opportunity to look at the document I have now shown you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object to any testimony about this document, in that it suggests an extraneous criminal offence which is not admissible under Rule 92 -- excuse me, your Honour, Rule 93; I am sorry, Rule 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What does Rule 93 say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Rule 93 is an exception to the general rule that proof of other crimes is inadmissible. The exception is if it is a consistent pattern of violations of international humanitarian law recognisable under the Statute it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think this is proving anything like that against him. Even what this contains is accusation. This establishes nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I should make it clear that in the Prosecution -- the Prosecution does not seek to tender this in relation to the truth of any of the allegations contained in it. It is not sought to do that for that purpose at all. I make the observation, your Honours, that it does not face the objection that one might have, should it be a finding of a court which the Prosecution or a party may press upon your Honours to be a finding that your Honours should accept, but nevertheless, even though it does not go to that, in any event the Prosecution seeks to tender this on the basis that it refers to the persons mentioned and the ranks, responsibilities and duties ascribed to them by the document itself. That is the basis upon which the Prosecution seeks to tender it. It does not seek to, in any way, rely upon the allegations made therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: From this there is another aspect. This document explains why the General had requested that the warrant be issued, this document which is a report to the chief of staff. It does not mention why a warrant was being sought against the -- against Zejnil Delalic. This document explains why, what were the charges against him. In fact, you should welcome this particular document, instead of opposing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would normally, except this accuses my client of a murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It may be. But that is nothing to do with us. He has not been charged with the murder of Nurko Delalil. This in fact explains the request by the General to his superior that warrants be issued for his arrest. In fact, you should welcome this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In the normal course of business I would. Any probative value it has is clearly outweighed by the prejudicial value of calling my guy a murderer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is merely an allegation, it has not been said it has been proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, it is merely an allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: An allegation I ask your Honours to disregard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with us. I accept there are other facts which may be relevant to the charges against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why is it that you are able to recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise this document for its contents and because here there is my name, first and last name, after I have reported to the chief of staff of the Supreme Command and asked for a warrant of arrest to be issued. I received an approval that I could undertake criminal proceedings, that is, to ask for a criminal charges against these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. And the persons that are named therein, namely Zejnil Delalic, Esad -- Zejnil Delalic, Hazim Delic, Zdravko Mucic also known as Pavo, are they persons who were the subject of your investigation as was referred to in the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are the duties and ranks ascribed to those persons in this document, so far as you are aware, correct for the time, at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, we had no ranks, we only had duties, but the committee that performed -- that carried out the investigation informed me that against these persons criminal charges should be started, and I did it at the District Military Court under the orders of the chief of staff, of the general staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: General, my question was: so far as you are aware, were the positions ascribed to the persons named in this document correct, so far as you are concerned, or were aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender this document, your Honour. The truth of its contents in relation to the limited purpose of the names and the positions that are ascribed to the persons contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I would just like to ask a question of the General at this stage. These charges were prepared on the basis of the report of the commission that you had set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the report of the commission, which carried out investigations, the investigative proceedings, and on the basis of the approval of the chief of staff, because I cannot press any charges or start any proceedings if I have not received the approval of my superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am almost finished. I have some more questions and some more documents, but there is not much more of my evidence to go, but I note the time. Would your Honours wish to rise now, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It depends how much longer you intend to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is going to be at least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, we can conclude tomorrow morning, so that cross-examination can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before you leave, just as a matter of planning, I might inquire of the Prosecutor, it appears that this witness' testimony will probably go through the day tomorrow. Does the Prosecutor intend to continue calling the current list of witnesses into next week? It seems apparent that is where we are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The best I can answer at the moment, your Honours, is that the witnesses are on subpoena, so it may be that we need to see, if they go back to Sarajevo, whether they will come back again. That may be a matter which we may need to spend some time on tomorrow afternoon, resolving. So to answer the question, we will proceed on -- our intention is to proceed on Monday, with witnesses who have been subject to subpoena, for that one day only. We have the other witness that we would be seeking to take the evidence from, Professor Economides. Professor Gow we have been able to move to another week. I say this, your Honour, knowing that I have not got your Honour's leave to call these witnesses, but, because I have been asked a question about timing, this is our plan. So Professor Gow would go over to the following week, and we would proceed on Monday with these witnesses, and then the next witness would be ^ name Professor Economides merely because he needs -- that is the only time he has available to testify. Then we would resume with the witnesses subject to subpoena. Then, on the following Monday, the evidence of Gow. That is about the best estimate I am able to give at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a concern with respect to Professor Gow that I want to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber so it does not look like we are sneaking up on the Trial Chamber in some way. There is an enormous list of publications by Dr. Gow regarding the war in Yugoslavia. We would be remiss in our duties to our clients if we did not acquire copies of all those publications and study them before cross-examining him. We have been unwilling to expend the Tribunal's money in gathering those documents. It will be a very, very expensive process, until the issue of whether or not the Trial Chamber is going to permit the Prosecution to call him or not has been decided. And so there is a timing problem that I would like the Chamber to be aware of. The documents are very, very extensive, and very, very expensive to gather together. That is a concern we are all sharing at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you really need every publication?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not every publication, just every writing that he has done with regard to the war in Yugoslavia. I do not care about his writings about the Gulf war, but his writings about Yugoslavia I would like ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it helped the court, I can say that there are 15 writings in the Jayne’s' publications alone related to Yugoslavia. But I also have a concern related to Professor Economides; I spent a good deal of yesterday on the Internet trying to find out about Professor Economides and he is supposedly on some organisation or commission for democracy of law in Europe, that kind of thing. I found one reference to Professor Economides, which is he is on some totally different commission in Europe. I found no references at all to the Commission for Law and Democracy in Europe. He is supposedly the reporter for a nationality citizenship study done by that Commission and I cannot find anything out about it. I think that would probably be highly relevant to his testimony. I would sure like to have that. I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are doubting his expertise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know what I know about him. I just told you everything I know about the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you fear that he might be useful why do you bother?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I say, your Honour, it would be useful to me if he had some prior writings on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thus if he has no real authority on what he is saying, why do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To assist Mr. Moran on this matter, he is on the United Nations International Law Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand he is now on the ILC, but that documents given to us by the Office of the Prosecutor, relayed to me by Mr. Ackerman while I was in Houston, listed this other organisation that I cannot find anything about, and that he was the reporter for a study that was done on nationalities and citizenship. I think that would probably be one of the documents I would like to get my hands on. If the Prosecutor has it, I would be happy to borrow it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not have it. If I can obtain access to it, I would be quite happy to share it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What we are not sure is are the Defence willing to argue the motion for allowing the experts to be called? I think that makes life easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be prepared to do it at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning. There is a document sitting in my hotel room that I would like to be able to copy and hand to the Trial Chamber, that relates, I think, directly to one of the two proposed experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we will dispose of it tomorrow morning. Then we will know where we stand. Okay. The Trial Chamber will now rise.
